docs.title: DAX Reference Library
docs.text:
A curated reference library of reusable DAX patterns for Power BI.

The purpose of this site is to provide concise, practical guidance for common analytical calculations while explaining the underlying DAX behaviour, particularly around filter context, hierarchy handling and reusable measure design.

Only mature, reusable patterns suitable for general use are published here.

Examples are intentionally generic and should be adapted to the semantic model and business requirements of the implementation in which they are used.

docs.title: Filter Context Patterns
docs.text: Reusable DAX patterns for deliberately manipulating, preserving and removing filter context.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
ID Pattern Difficulty Description 004 Ignore a Specific Filter Basic / Intermediate Evaluate a measure while deliberately removing one filter and preserving the remaining report context. 005 Keep Only Specific Filters Intermediate Remove filters from a dimension while explicitly preserving one or more required grouping filters using ALLEXCEPT.

← Back to DAX Reference Library

docs.title: DAX Pattern 004 — Ignore a Specific Filter
Purpose
docs.text:
Calculate a measure while deliberately ignoring one specific filter but preserving the rest of the current report context.

This is useful when a calculation should remain responsive to most slicers and filters while being unaffected by one particular dimension or attribute.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use this pattern when:

  • A measure should ignore one slicer or visual grouping.
  • A benchmark or baseline should remain constant across one dimension.
  • A calculation should preserve filters such as Year, Region or Channel while ignoring Product Category.
  • A comparison requires the current value and a reference value evaluated under different filter contexts.

docs.title: Business Example
docs.text:
Assume a report shows sales by Product Category:

Category Sales Clothing £500,000 Footwear £300,000 Accessories £200,000 Total £1,000,000

The report also contains filters for:

Year = 2026
Region = North

The requirement is to show total sales for the selected Year and Region while ignoring whichever Category is currently displayed.

The expected result is:

Category Sales Sales Ignoring Category Clothing £500,000 £1,000,000 Footwear £300,000 £1,000,000 Accessories £200,000 £1,000,000

The reference value remains the same for each category because the Category filter is deliberately removed.

docs.title: Base Measure
docs.text:
Use an existing reusable base measure:

Total Sales =
SUM ( Sales[Sales Amount] )

docs.title: DAX Pattern
docs.text:
Sales Ignoring Category =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
)

docs.title: 1. Start with the Current Filter Context
docs.text:
Suppose the current visual row is:

Category = Clothing

and the report has:

Year   = 2026
Region = North

The original filter context is therefore:

Year     = 2026
Region   = North
Category = Clothing

[Total Sales] evaluated directly in this context returns:

£500,000

docs.title: 2. Modify the Filter Context
docs.text:
The measure uses:

CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
)

CALCULATE evaluates [Total Sales] under a modified filter context.

REMOVEFILTERS removes:

Category = Clothing

while leaving the other filters intact.

The resulting context is therefore:

Year     = 2026
Region   = North
Category = ALL

The result becomes:

£1,000,000

docs.title: Key Principle
docs.text:
This pattern does not mean:

Ignore all report filters.

It means:

Ignore this specific filter while retaining the remaining context.

That distinction is fundamental to reusable DAX design.

docs.title: Standard Measure
docs.text:
[Total Sales]

For Clothing:

Year     = 2026
Region   = North
Category = Clothing

Result = £500,000

docs.title: Filter-Removal Measure
docs.text:
[Sales Ignoring Category]

For Clothing:

Year     = 2026
Region   = North
Category = ALL

Result = £1,000,000

Only the intended filter has changed.

docs.title: Why Use CALCULATE?
docs.text:
CALCULATE is one of the most important DAX functions because it allows an expression to be evaluated under a modified filter context.

Conceptually:

Existing filter context
        ↓
CALCULATE
        ↓
Apply filter changes
        ↓
Evaluate expression

For this pattern:

Current context
        ↓
Remove Product[Category]
        ↓
Evaluate [Total Sales]

The aggregation itself has not changed.

The context in which the aggregation is evaluated has changed.

docs.title: Column-Level Filter Removal
docs.text:
This pattern deliberately uses:

REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )

rather than:

REMOVEFILTERS ( Product )

The difference is significant.

docs.title: Column-Level Removal
docs.text:
REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )

removes only the Category filter.

Other Product-table filters may remain active.

docs.title: Table-Level Removal
docs.text:
REMOVEFILTERS ( Product )

removes filters from the entire Product table.

That could unintentionally remove filters such as:

Brand
Department
Product
Season

Use the narrowest filter-removal scope that satisfies the business requirement.

docs.title: Example with Multiple Filters
docs.text:
Assume the report context is:

Year       = 2026
Region     = North
Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses

The measure:

Sales Ignoring Category =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
)

changes the evaluation context to:

Year       = 2026
Region     = North
Department = Womenswear
Category   = ALL

The Department filter remains active.

The result therefore represents:

Sales for all categories within Womenswear, North, during 2026.

docs.title: Benchmark Against a Wider Group
docs.text: Compare an individual category with the wider Department total.

docs.title: Fixed Reference Line
docs.text: Create a reference value that remains constant across a visual axis.

docs.title: Ignore a Slicer
docs.text: Allow a measure to disregard a specific selection while other measures continue to respond to it.

docs.title: Comparative Measures
docs.text: Create a current-context value and a broader-context comparison value.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
This pattern assumes:

  • A reusable base measure already exists.
  • The filter to be removed can be clearly identified.
  • Other report filters should remain active.
  • The semantic model contains appropriate dimension relationships.
  • Removing the specified filter produces the intended analytical context.

docs.title: Removing Too Much Context
docs.text:
Using:

REMOVEFILTERS ()

or removing an entire table may produce a denominator or reference value that ignores important report selections.

docs.title: Removing the Wrong Column
docs.text:
The filter being removed must correspond to the business question.

For example:

REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )

and:

REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Department] )

answer different analytical questions.

docs.title: Assuming Visual Layout Equals Filter Context
docs.text:
A column appearing in a visual does not necessarily mean it is the only filter affecting the measure.

Slicers, page filters, report filters and cross-filtering can all contribute to the current context.

docs.title: Repeating Aggregation Logic
docs.text:
Prefer:

CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
)

rather than repeating:

SUM ( Sales[Sales Amount] )

inside every dependent measure.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
This pattern is generally inexpensive in a well-designed star schema.

Good practice includes:

  • Removing filters from dimension columns rather than large fact tables.
  • Reusing existing base measures.
  • Keeping filter manipulation as narrow as possible.
  • Avoiding unnecessary iterator functions.
  • Testing behaviour in visuals containing multiple interacting filters.

The main consideration is usually analytical correctness rather than computational cost.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Depending on the requirement, related functions include:

docs.title: ALL
docs.text: Can also remove filters and is commonly encountered in existing DAX.

docs.title: ALLSELECTED
docs.text: Useful when the calculation should preserve the user's wider selected set.

docs.title: ALLEXCEPT
docs.text: Useful when most filters on a table should be removed while explicitly preserving selected columns.

docs.title: Explicit Filter Expressions
docs.text:
CALCULATE can also add or replace filters directly rather than only removing them.

These approaches should be chosen according to the required filter behaviour rather than syntax preference.

docs.title: Relationship to Percentage Patterns
docs.text:
Pattern 001 — Percentage of Total uses this same principle when calculating its denominator:

CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
)

The difference is that Pattern 004 isolates the filter-context technique itself.

This makes it reusable for many calculations that have nothing to do with percentages.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
• Percentage of Total
  • Percentage of Selected Total
  • Preserve Selected Filters
  • Remove All Filters from a Dimension
  • Keep Only Specific Filters
  • Fixed Benchmark Measure

docs.title: Classification
docs.text: Attribute Value Type Measure Pattern Category Filter Context Difficulty Basic / Intermediate Context Dependency High Reusability High Performance Sensitivity Low

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The key concept in this pattern is:

DAX calculations are often changed not by altering the aggregation, but by changing the filter context in which that aggregation is evaluated.

Understanding deliberate filter removal is foundational to more advanced use of CALCULATE.

docs.text:

docs.title: DAX Pattern 005 — Keep Only Specific Filter
Purpose
docs.text:
Evaluate a measure while removing most filters from a table but deliberately preserving one or more specified filters.

This pattern is useful when a calculation should ignore lower-level or unrelated filters within a dimension while retaining a defined grouping context.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use this pattern when:

  • A calculation should preserve one hierarchy level while ignoring lower levels.
  • A benchmark should remain fixed within a Department, Region or other grouping.
  • A measure should remove most filters from a dimension table but keep selected columns active.
  • The intended comparison set is defined by a specific parent or grouping attribute.
  • Repeating multiple REMOVEFILTERS expressions would be less clear than explicitly preserving the required filters.

docs.title: Business Example
docs.text:
Assume a Product dimension contains:

Department
Category
Product
Brand

A report shows Product-level sales within Department.

Example:

Department Category Product Sales Womenswear Dresses Product A £200,000 Womenswear Dresses Product B £300,000 Womenswear Knitwear Product C £250,000 Womenswear Knitwear Product D £250,000

The requirement is to calculate total Womenswear sales for every Product row while ignoring Category and Product.

The required reference value is:

Womenswear Total Sales = £1,000,000

For each Product row:

Product Sales Department Sales Product A £200,000 £1,000,000 Product B £300,000 £1,000,000 Product C £250,000 £1,000,000 Product D £250,000 £1,000,000

docs.title: Base Measure
docs.text:
Use the existing base measure:

Total Sales =
SUM ( Sales[Sales Amount] )

docs.title: DAX Pattern
docs.text:
Sales Within Department =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    ALLEXCEPT (
        Product,
        Product[Department]
    )
)

docs.title: 1. Start with the Current Filter Context
docs.text:
Suppose the current visual row is:

Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses
Product    = Product A

The current measure:

[Total Sales]

returns:

£200,000

because all three filters contribute to the current context.

docs.title: 2. Preserve Only the Required Filter
docs.text:
The expression:

ALLEXCEPT (
    Product,
    Product[Department]
)

removes filters from the Product table except for:

Product[Department]

The context therefore changes from:

Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses
Product    = Product A

to:

Department = Womenswear
Category   = ALL
Product    = ALL

The calculation then returns:

£1,000,000

for total Womenswear sales.

docs.title: Key Principle
docs.text:
ALLEXCEPT can be understood as:

Remove filters from this table except for the filters I explicitly want to preserve.

Conceptually:

Current Product filters
        ↓
Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses
Product    = Product A
        ↓
ALLEXCEPT
        ↓
Keep Department
Remove Category
Remove Product
        ↓
Department = Womenswear

docs.title: Why Use ALLEXCEPT?
docs.text:
The same business outcome could sometimes be achieved using multiple filter-removal expressions.

For example:

Sales Within Department =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] ),
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Product] )
)

However, if the Product table contains many additional attributes such as:

Brand
Season
Collection
Colour
Range
Supplier

the expression may become harder to maintain.

ALLEXCEPT expresses the intent from the opposite direction:

Remove everything from Product except Department.

This can be clearer when the preserved context is simpler than the set of filters to remove.

docs.title: Filter-Context Behaviour
docs.text:
Assume the report context contains:

Year       = 2026
Region     = North
Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses
Product    = Product A

The measure:

Sales Within Department =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    ALLEXCEPT (
        Product,
        Product[Department]
    )
)

produces:

Year       = 2026
Region     = North
Department = Womenswear
Category   = ALL
Product    = ALL

Notice that:

Year
Region

remain active because ALLEXCEPT is applied only to the Product table.

docs.title: Preserving More Than One Filter
docs.text:
ALLEXCEPT can preserve multiple columns from the same table.

For example:

Sales Within Department and Brand =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    ALLEXCEPT (
        Product,
        Product[Department],
        Product[Brand]
    )
)

This removes other Product filters while preserving:

Department
Brand

The resulting measure answers:

What are total sales within the current Department and Brand combination?

docs.title: Comparison with Pattern 004
docs.text:
Pattern 004 uses:

REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )

and means:

Remove this specific filter.

Pattern 005 uses:

ALLEXCEPT (
    Product,
    Product[Department]
)

and means:

Remove filters from this table except for this specific filter.

The choice depends on which description is simpler and more closely matches the business requirement.

docs.title: Example Comparison
docs.text:
Assume the current Product context is:

Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses
Brand      = Brand A
Product    = Product A

docs.title: Remove Category Only
docs.text:
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
)

Resulting context:

Department = Womenswear
Category   = ALL
Brand      = Brand A
Product    = Product A

Other Product filters remain.

docs.title: Preserve Department Only
docs.text:
CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    ALLEXCEPT (
        Product,
        Product[Department]
    )
)

Resulting context:

Department = Womenswear
Category   = ALL
Brand      = ALL
Product    = ALL

These two calculations answer very different business questions.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
This pattern assumes:

  • The filters being manipulated belong to the same dimension table.
  • The filter or filters to preserve are clearly defined.
  • Other filters on that dimension should be removed.
  • Filters from unrelated dimensions should remain active.
  • The semantic model relationships are correctly configured.
  • The preserved column provides a meaningful analytical grouping.

docs.title: Preserving Too Little Context
docs.text:
Using:

ALLEXCEPT (
    Product,
    Product[Department]
)

will remove every other Product-table filter.

If Brand or Season should remain active, they must also be preserved.

docs.title: Assuming External Filters Are Removed
docs.text:
ALLEXCEPT only operates on the specified table.

For example:

Date
Region
Customer
Channel

filters remain active unless explicitly changed elsewhere.

docs.title: Using ALLEXCEPT Automatically for Parent Totals
docs.text:
A parent-total requirement does not always mean ALLEXCEPT is appropriate.

Sometimes a more targeted:

REMOVEFILTERS

expression is easier to understand and less likely to remove useful context.

Choose the function according to the required filter behaviour.

docs.title: Using It Across Unrelated Tables
docs.text:
The preserved columns passed to ALLEXCEPT must belong to the table being supplied as its first argument.

For example:

ALLEXCEPT (
    Product,
    Product[Department],
    Region[Region]
)

is not a valid way to preserve filters from unrelated tables.

docs.title: When REMOVEFILTERS May Be Clearer
docs.text:
Suppose the only requirement is:

Ignore Category but keep all other Product filters.

Then this is explicit:

REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )

Using:

ALLEXCEPT

would require identifying every Product filter that should remain active.

In this scenario, Pattern 004 is generally clearer.

docs.title: When ALLEXCEPT May Be Clearer
docs.text:
Suppose the requirement is:

Ignore all Product-level detail but keep Department.

Then:

ALLEXCEPT (
    Product,
    Product[Department]
)

expresses that requirement directly.

The preferred implementation should communicate the analytical intent as clearly as possible.

docs.title: Department-Level Benchmark
docs.text: Show a Department total alongside lower-level Category or Product rows.

docs.title: Regional Benchmark
docs.text: Remove lower-level geographic filters while preserving Region.

docs.title: Customer-Segment Analysis
docs.text: Preserve Customer Segment while ignoring individual Customer filters.

docs.title: Parent-Level Comparison
docs.text: Create a reference value at a specified parent grouping.

docs.title: Stable Group Baseline
docs.text: Create a baseline that remains constant within a defined group.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
This pattern is generally efficient in a well-designed dimensional model.

Consider:

  • Applying ALLEXCEPT to dimension tables rather than large fact tables.
  • Preserving only the columns required by the business rule.
  • Reusing existing base measures.
  • Avoiding unnecessary filter manipulation.
  • Testing behaviour where the dimension contains many attributes and interacting slicers.

The main risk is usually unintended filter removal rather than computational cost.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Depending on the requirement, alternatives include:

docs.title: REMOVEFILTERS
docs.text: Prefer when only one or a small number of known filters need to be removed.

docs.title: ALL
docs.text: Can remove filters from a table or column and is frequently encountered in existing DAX.

docs.title: ALLSELECTED
docs.text: Prefer when the wider user-selected comparison set must be retained.

docs.title: Explicit CALCULATE Filters
docs.text:
Useful where filters need to be added, replaced or precisely controlled.

The correct implementation depends on the business meaning of the required evaluation context.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:

  • Percentage of Parent
  • Preserve Selected Filters
  • Remove All Filters from a Dimension
  • Fixed Group Benchmark

docs.text: Attribute Value Type Measure Pattern Category Filter Context Difficulty Intermediate Context Dependency High Reusability High Performance Sensitivity Low

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The key concept in this pattern is:

ALLEXCEPT defines filter context by identifying what should remain rather than listing everything that should be removed.

Use it when the preserved grouping is clearer and more stable than the set of filters that must be removed.

docs.title: Percentage Patterns
docs.text: Reusable DAX patterns for percentage contribution, selected totals and hierarchical percentage calculations.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
ID Pattern Difficulty Description 001 Percentage of Total Basic / Intermediate Calculate an item's contribution to a total by modifying the denominator's filter context. 002 Percentage of Selected Total Intermediate Calculate contribution within the user's currently selected comparison set using ALLSELECTED. 003 Percentage of Parent Intermediate Calculate contribution to the immediate parent dynamically across hierarchy levels using ISINSCOPE.

← Back to DAX Reference Library

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Calculate the contribution of the current item relative to its immediate parent within a hierarchy.

A common example is calculating:

  • Product as a percentage of Category.
  • Category as a percentage of Department.
  • Department as a percentage of Total.

This pattern is useful when the denominator needs to change depending on the hierarchy level currently being displayed.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use this pattern when:

  • A matrix or hierarchical visual contains multiple levels.
  • The denominator must represent the current item's immediate parent.
  • Percentage contribution should be meaningful at each hierarchy level.
  • A single measure needs to behave differently depending on drill level.

docs.title: Business Example
docs.text:
Assume the hierarchy is:

Department
    ↓
Category
    ↓
Product

Example data:

Department Category Product Sales Womenswear Dresses Product A £200,000 Womenswear Dresses Product B £300,000 Womenswear Knitwear Product C £250,000 Womenswear Knitwear Product D £250,000

Totals:

Womenswear        £1,000,000

Dresses             £500,000
Knitwear            £500,000

Product A           £200,000
Product B           £300,000
Product C           £250,000
Product D           £250,000

The required percentages are:

Product A = 40% of Dresses
Product B = 60% of Dresses

Dresses   = 50% of Womenswear
Knitwear  = 50% of Womenswear

The denominator therefore changes depending on the current hierarchy level.

docs.title: Base Measure
docs.text:
Use the existing base measure:

Total Sales =
SUM ( Sales[Sales Amount] )

docs.title: DAX Pattern
docs.text:
Sales % of Parent =
VAR CurrentSales =
    [Total Sales]

VAR ParentSales =
    SWITCH (
        TRUE (),

        ISINSCOPE ( Product[Product] ),
            CALCULATE (
                [Total Sales],
                REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Product] )
            ),

        ISINSCOPE ( Product[Category] ),
            CALCULATE (
                [Total Sales],
                REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
            ),

        ISINSCOPE ( Product[Department] ),
            CALCULATE (
                [Total Sales],
                REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Department] )
            )
    )

RETURN
    DIVIDE (
        CurrentSales,
        ParentSales
    )

docs.title: 1. Determine the Current Hierarchy Level
docs.text:
The measure uses:

ISINSCOPE ( ... )

to identify which hierarchy level is currently being evaluated.

For example:

ISINSCOPE ( Product[Product] )

returns TRUE when the visual is currently evaluating an individual product row.

Likewise:

ISINSCOPE ( Product[Category] )

returns TRUE when the current evaluation level is Category.

docs.title: 2. Product-Level Calculation
docs.text:
If the current row is:

Product A

the measure evaluates:

CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Product] )
)

This removes the product-level filter while retaining the Category and Department filters.

The context therefore changes from:

Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses
Product    = Product A

to:

Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses
Product    = ALL

The denominator becomes total sales for Dresses:

£500,000

Therefore:

£200,000
────────── = 40%
£500,000

docs.title: 3. Category-Level Calculation
docs.text:
If the current row is:

Dresses

the measure evaluates:

CALCULATE (
    [Total Sales],
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
)

The context changes from:

Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses

to:

Department = Womenswear
Category   = ALL

The denominator becomes:

Womenswear sales = £1,000,000

Therefore:

£500,000
────────── = 50%
£1,000,000

docs.title: 4. Department-Level Calculation
docs.text:
At Department level:

REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Department] )

removes the Department restriction.

The denominator therefore becomes the relevant higher-level total within the remaining filter context.

docs.title: Why ISINSCOPE Is Important
docs.text:
A hierarchy can produce different filter combinations depending on:

  • Drill level.
  • Expand/collapse state.
  • Matrix structure.
  • Subtotals.
  • Report filters.

Simply checking whether a column is filtered is not always sufficient.

ISINSCOPE is designed to identify whether a hierarchy column is currently participating as the active grouping level in the visual.

This makes it particularly useful for hierarchy-aware measures.

docs.title: Evaluation Order
docs.text:
The order of the SWITCH conditions matters.

The measure checks the most detailed level first:

Product
↓
Category
↓
Department

This is necessary because when Product is in scope, Category and Department may also form part of the wider filter context.

The measure should therefore detect the lowest active hierarchy level first.

docs.title: Filter-Context Behaviour
docs.text:
At Product level:

Numerator:
Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses
Product    = Product A

Denominator:
Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses
Product    = ALL

At Category level:

Numerator:
Department = Womenswear
Category   = Dresses

Denominator:
Department = Womenswear
Category   = ALL

The result is always:

Current item ÷ immediate parent total

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
This pattern assumes:

  • A recognised hierarchy exists.
  • The hierarchy levels are stored in dimension columns.
  • [Total Sales] already exists.
  • The hierarchy is evaluated from higher to lower levels.
  • Removing the current-level filter produces the required immediate parent context.
  • Model relationships are correctly configured.

docs.title: Checking Hierarchy Levels in the Wrong Order
docs.text:
This can cause the measure to return the wrong denominator.

Always test the most detailed level first.

docs.title: Removing Too Many Filters
docs.text: For Product percentage of Category, removing Category as well as Product would calculate Product as a percentage of Department rather than Category.

docs.title: Using HASONEVALUE as a Substitute
docs.text:
HASONEVALUE answers whether one value exists in the current filter context.

That is not the same question as whether a column is the active hierarchy level.

For hierarchy-aware calculations, ISINSCOPE is usually the clearer choice.

docs.title: Ignoring Subtotals
docs.text:
Hierarchy measures should always be tested against:

  • Detail rows.
  • Parent rows.
  • Subtotals.
  • Grand totals.

The required subtotal behaviour should be explicitly defined.

docs.title: Grand Total Behaviour
docs.text:
At the grand-total level, none of the hierarchy columns may be in scope.

In that situation:

ParentSales

may evaluate to BLANK().

The resulting percentage will therefore also return blank.

This is often desirable because a grand total being "a percentage of its parent" may have no meaningful business interpretation.

If the requirement is to show:

100%

at the grand total, that behaviour should be added deliberately rather than assumed.

docs.title: Optional Grand Total Version
docs.text:
If the requirement is for the grand total to display 100%, the pattern can be extended:

Sales % of Parent =
VAR CurrentSales =
    [Total Sales]

VAR ParentSales =
    SWITCH (
        TRUE (),

        ISINSCOPE ( Product[Product] ),
            CALCULATE (
                [Total Sales],
                REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Product] )
            ),

        ISINSCOPE ( Product[Category] ),
            CALCULATE (
                [Total Sales],
                REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
            ),

        ISINSCOPE ( Product[Department] ),
            CALCULATE (
                [Total Sales],
                REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Department] )
            ),

        [Total Sales]
    )

RETURN
    DIVIDE (
        CurrentSales,
        ParentSales
    )

At grand total:

Current Sales ÷ Current Sales = 100%

Use this variation only where the business presentation requires it.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
This pattern is generally inexpensive for standard dimensional models.

Consider:

  • Keeping hierarchy columns within a proper dimension table.
  • Using reusable base measures.
  • Avoiding unnecessary iterators.
  • Limiting filter removal to the relevant hierarchy column.
  • Testing matrix behaviour where the hierarchy contains many members.

The complexity of this pattern is primarily contextual rather than computational.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
Depending on the model and hierarchy design, alternatives may include:

  • Separate measures for each hierarchy level.
  • Explicit CALCULATE logic tied to individual visuals.
  • ALLSELECTED when the parent denominator must respect a user-defined selected set.
  • Calculation groups for reusable hierarchy-aware behaviour.

A single ISINSCOPE measure is particularly useful when one measure needs to adapt dynamically across hierarchy levels.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:

  • Percentage of Selected Total
  • Percentage Within Group
  • Hierarchy-Aware Variance
  • Dynamic Matrix Measures

docs.text: Attribute Value Type Measure Pattern Category Percentages Difficulty Intermediate Context Dependency High Reusability High Performance Sensitivity Low

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The key concept in this pattern is:

The denominator is determined by the hierarchy level currently in scope.

ISINSCOPE identifies that level, while CALCULATE and REMOVEFILTERS create the appropriate parent context.

This allows one measure to behave intelligently across multiple drill levels.

docs.title: DAX Pattern 002 — Percentage of Selected Total
Purpose
docs.text:
Calculate the contribution of the current item to the total represented by the user's current selection.

This pattern is useful when slicers or report selections define the comparison set and the denominator should reflect only those selected values.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use this pattern when you need to calculate:

  • Percentage contribution within a slicer selection.
  • Share of currently selected categories, products or regions.
  • Dynamic percentage-of-total calculations that respond to user selections.
  • Contribution within the visible selection rather than against the broader model total.

docs.title: Business Example
docs.text:
Assume the full model contains:

Category Sales Clothing £500,000 Footwear £300,000 Accessories £200,000 Total £1,000,000

The report user selects only:

Clothing
Footwear

The selected total is therefore:

£800,000

The required result becomes:

Category Sales % of Selected Total Clothing £500,000 62.5% Footwear £300,000 37.5% Selected Total £800,000 100%

Accessories is not part of the selected comparison set.

docs.title: Base Measure
docs.text:
Use the existing reusable measure:

Total Sales =
SUM ( Sales[Sales Amount] )

docs.title: DAX Pattern
docs.text:
Sales % of Selected Total =
VAR CurrentSales =
    [Total Sales]

VAR SelectedCategorySales =
    CALCULATE (
        [Total Sales],
        ALLSELECTED ( Product[Category] )
    )

RETURN
    DIVIDE (
        CurrentSales,
        SelectedCategorySales
    )

docs.title: 1. Calculate the Current Value
docs.text:
VAR CurrentSales =
    [Total Sales]

For the Clothing row, the current evaluation context includes:

Product[Category] = "Clothing"

The result is therefore:

CurrentSales = £500,000

docs.title: 2. Calculate the Selected Denominator
docs.text:
VAR SelectedCategorySales =
    CALCULATE (
        [Total Sales],
        ALLSELECTED ( Product[Category] )
    )

ALLSELECTED removes the row-level category filter while retaining the broader selection made by the report user.

If the user has selected:

Clothing
Footwear

then the denominator becomes:

£500,000 + £300,000 = £800,000

Accessories remains excluded because it was not selected.

docs.title: Filter-Context Behaviour
docs.text: The numerator and denominator are evaluated differently.

docs.title: Numerator
docs.text:
For Clothing:

Current row:
Category = Clothing

User selection:
Clothing
Footwear

Result:

£500,000

docs.title: Denominator
docs.text:
The row-level category restriction is removed, but the wider user selection is retained:

Selected categories:
Clothing
Footwear

Result:

£800,000

The final calculation is therefore:

£500,000
────────── = 0.625 = 62.5%
 £800,000

docs.title: Difference from Pattern 001
docs.text:
Pattern 001 uses:

REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )

Pattern 002 uses:

ALLSELECTED ( Product[Category] )

These are not interchangeable.

docs.title: Pattern 001 — Percentage of Total
docs.text:
The denominator removes the current category filter.

Depending on the wider report context, this can evaluate against all available categories.

docs.title: Pattern 002 — Percentage of Selected Total
docs.text:
The denominator respects the broader selection made by the report user.

This allows the comparison set itself to change dynamically.

docs.title: Example Comparison
docs.text:
Assume the full dataset is:

Clothing     £500,000
Footwear     £300,000
Accessories  £200,000

The user selects:

Clothing
Footwear

For Clothing:

docs.title: Percentage of Selected Total
docs.text:
£500,000 / £800,000 = 62.5%

The correct pattern therefore depends on the business question being asked.

docs.title: Business Questions
docs.text:
Pattern 001 answers:

What percentage of the relevant total does this item represent?

Pattern 002 answers:

What percentage of the currently selected comparison set does this item represent?

That distinction should be established before choosing the DAX implementation.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
This pattern assumes:

  • [Total Sales] already exists.
  • Product[Category] defines the members being compared.
  • The report allows users to filter or select category values.
  • The denominator should respect the user's selected comparison set.
  • The semantic model relationships are correctly configured.

docs.title: Using ALLSELECTED Without a Clear Requirement
docs.text:
ALLSELECTED should not be used simply because a report contains slicers.

The analytical requirement must specifically call for the denominator to reflect the selected comparison set.

docs.title: Assuming ALLSELECTED Means "Everything Visible"
docs.text:
Its behaviour depends on evaluation context and can become less intuitive in complex visuals or nested calculations.

Always validate the result against the intended business meaning.

docs.title: Confusing Row Context with Selection Context
docs.text:
The current row in a visual and the broader user selection are separate contextual concepts.

This pattern deliberately removes the former while retaining the latter.

docs.title: Repeating Base Aggregation Logic
docs.text:
Continue to use measure branching:

Total Sales
    ↓
Sales % of Selected Total

rather than reproducing aggregation logic in every dependent measure.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
For normal dimensional models, this pattern is generally inexpensive.

Consider:

  • Keeping the filter target specific.
  • Using established dimension columns for filtering.
  • Avoiding unnecessary iteration.
  • Testing ALLSELECTED carefully in complex report pages containing multiple interacting filters.

The main risk with this pattern is usually semantic correctness rather than raw performance.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
Depending on the requirement, alternatives include:

  • REMOVEFILTERS
  • ALL
  • ALLEXCEPT
  • Explicit filter expressions within CALCULATE

The appropriate function depends on which filters should be removed and which must remain active.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The main lesson from this pattern is:

ALLSELECTED is useful when the denominator should reflect the user's active comparison set rather than the broader available total.

The business meaning of the denominator should always be defined before selecting the DAX function.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Calculate the contribution of the current item to a total while retaining the filter context that defines the required analysis.

A common example is calculating each product category's sales as a percentage of total sales.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use this pattern when you need to calculate:

  • Percentage of total sales by product, category or region.
  • Percentage contribution to an overall value.
  • Share of revenue, cost, quantity or another additive measure.
  • Relative contribution of individual members within a dimension.

docs.title: Business Example
docs.text:
Assume a report contains sales by product category:

Category Sales Clothing £500,000 Footwear £300,000 Accessories £200,000 Total £1,000,000

The required result is:

Category Sales % of Total Clothing £500,000 50% Footwear £300,000 30% Accessories £200,000 20% Total £1,000,000 100%

docs.title: Base Measure
docs.text:
Start with a reusable base measure:

Total Sales =
SUM ( Sales[Sales Amount] )

This measure returns sales within the current filter context.

docs.title: DAX Pattern
docs.text:
Sales % of Total =
VAR CurrentSales =
    [Total Sales]

VAR AllCategorySales =
    CALCULATE (
        [Total Sales],
        REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
    )

RETURN
    DIVIDE (
        CurrentSales,
        AllCategorySales
    )

docs.title: 1. Calculate the Current Value
docs.text:
VAR CurrentSales =
    [Total Sales]

When the measure is evaluated against a category such as Clothing, the current filter context includes:

Product[Category] = "Clothing"

[Total Sales] therefore returns sales for Clothing.

In the example:

CurrentSales = £500,000

docs.title: 2. Calculate the Denominator
docs.text:
VAR AllCategorySales =
    CALCULATE (
        [Total Sales],
        REMOVEFILTERS ( Product[Category] )
    )

CALCULATE evaluates [Total Sales] using a modified filter context.

REMOVEFILTERS removes the filter specifically from:

Product[Category]

The category currently being displayed therefore no longer restricts the calculation.

For Clothing:

Current context:

Category = Clothing
        ↓
Total Sales = £500,000


Denominator context:

Category filter removed
        ↓
Total Sales = £1,000,000

Other report filters remain active unless they also affect the filter being explicitly removed.

docs.title: 3. Divide the Current Value by the Total
docs.text:
DIVIDE (
    CurrentSales,
    AllCategorySales
)

For Clothing:

£500,000
────────── = 0.50 = 50%
£1,000,000

DIVIDE is preferred to the / operator for this pattern because it safely handles a zero or blank denominator.

docs.title: Filter-Context Behaviour
docs.text: The important principle is that the numerator and denominator are intentionally evaluated under different filter contexts.

docs.title: Numerator
docs.text:
Retains the current category filter:

Category = Clothing
Region   = North
Year     = 2026

docs.title: Denominator
docs.text:
Removes only the category filter:

Category = ALL
Region   = North
Year     = 2026

The result therefore answers:

What percentage of sales within the currently selected Region and Year came from this Category?

This distinction is important. The denominator is not necessarily the unrestricted total for the entire model.

docs.title: Why Not Remove Every Filter?
docs.text:
A broader expression could be written using:

REMOVEFILTERS ()

However, this removes filters much more widely and may cause the denominator to ignore report selections that should remain relevant.

For example, if the user selects:

Year = 2026
Region = North

the required percentage may be the category's contribution within North during 2026, not its contribution to sales across every region and every year.

Filter removal should therefore be deliberate and as specific as the analytical requirement allows.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
This pattern assumes:

  • [Total Sales] is an existing measure.
  • Product[Category] is the dimension attribute whose contribution is being calculated.
  • The data model contains appropriate relationships between Product and Sales.
  • Other relevant report filters should remain active.
  • The denominator represents the total across categories within the remaining filter context.

docs.title: Removing Too Many Filters
docs.text: Using a broad filter-removal expression can unintentionally ignore slicers and other report selections.

docs.title: Removing the Wrong Filter
docs.text: The denominator must remove the filter responsible for dividing the visual into the members being compared.

docs.title: Dividing Directly
docs.text:
Using:

CurrentSales / AllCategorySales

works when the denominator is valid, but DIVIDE provides safer handling of zero and blank denominators.

docs.title: Recalculating Business Logic
docs.text:
Avoid repeating:

SUM ( Sales[Sales Amount] )

throughout dependent measures when [Total Sales] already defines that business logic.

Prefer measure branching:

Total Sales
    ↓
Sales % of Total

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
This pattern is generally inexpensive when operating over a well-designed star schema.

Consider:

  • Removing filters from the required dimension column rather than unnecessarily broad portions of the model.
  • Reusing established base measures.
  • Maintaining appropriate dimension-to-fact relationships.
  • Avoiding unnecessary iterator functions when simple aggregation is sufficient.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
The precise implementation depends on the analytical requirement.

Related approaches may use:

  • REMOVEFILTERS
  • ALL
  • ALLSELECTED

These functions can produce materially different results depending on the report's filter context.

ALLSELECTED, for example, may be appropriate when the required denominator is the total represented by the user's current selection rather than the broader total available after removing a specific filter.

These should be treated as related patterns rather than interchangeable syntax.

docs.title: Related Patterns
docs.text:
Future related entries:

  • Percentage of Selected Total
  • Percentage of Parent
  • Percentage Variance
  • Dynamic Share of Total
  • Ranking by Percentage Contribution

docs.text: Attribute Value Type Measure Pattern Category Percentages Difficulty Basic / Intermediate Context Dependency High Reusability High Performance Sensitivity Low

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The key learning from this pattern is not the division itself.

The important DAX concept is:

Evaluate the numerator in the current filter context and deliberately modify the filter context for the denominator.

Understanding that behaviour provides a foundation for many more advanced DAX calculations.
